changelog.title: Improvements on the pull request overview in public preview
changelog.text: Your feedback has helped improve the new pull request Overview page since its November 5, 2026 public preview. Here’s what’s new! Clearer merge status and next steps Failed optional checks no longer make mergeable pull requests appear blocked. Previously missing merge requirements now show what needs attention. Readiness summary gives reviewers and visitors clearer guidance, including when no action is needed. Smoother review and comment interactions Checks and approvals now expand when clicked, instead of pinning a preview. Fixed overlapping previews and mobile interaction issues. Resolved review threads now collapse to keep completed conversations out of the way. Comments mentioning Copilot now better explain the action and selected model before submission. Activity details Force-push activity now links to the old and new commits so you can compare changes. Commit activity now includes timestamps so you can see when changes were made. Page layout and sidebar actions Source and target branches now stay visible on smaller screens. Edit links in the Development sidebar directly in Overview. Lock or unlock PR conversations directly in Overview. Fixed uneven spacing, misalignment, and sidebar gaps across screen sizes. Try the new overview page and give feedback To join, select the ✨ Try the Overview page button in the header. You can use the same menu to return to the classic overview during the preview. This preview is very much a starting point, not the finished pull request experience. Try it on your next pull request. What is easier to find? Where do you still lose context? What sends you back to the classic overview? Share your feedback and report issues in the overview preview feedback discussion . The post Improvements on the pull request overview in public preview appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: Enterprise Live Migrations from Azure DevOps generally available
changelog.text: Enterprise Live Migrations (ELM) from Azure DevOps Services to GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency is now generally available. You can move your repositories while your teams keep working, then cut over on your schedule. Manage migrations through the portal or CLI: Choose a guided experience in the Azure DevOps portal or script your migrations with the Azure DevOps CLI. Pre-migration validation and lifecycle tracking help you identify issues and monitor progress before cutover. Cut over on your schedule: ELM continuously syncs changes from Azure DevOps to GitHub, so developers can keep contributing throughout the migration. When you’re ready, complete the move with a brief cutover at a time that works for your teams. Bring your development history with you: ELM syncs Git history, branches, tags, and pull requests, including titles, descriptions, comments, and user history. Your Azure DevOps branch policies migrate as GitHub branch rulesets. Keep using Azure Boards and Azure Pipelines: You can have ELM create the Azure Boards connection and rewire Azure Pipelines to your migrated GitHub repository, reducing manual setup after cutover. Your work items and pipeline definitions stay in Azure DevOps. Ready to start your migration journey? Visit Microsoft’s ELM documentation to learn more and get started. The post Enterprise Live Migrations from Azure DevOps generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: Red Hat Enterprise Linux runner images now generally available
changelog.text: Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 9 and RHEL 10 images for GitHub-hosted larger runners are now generally available. Originally introduced in public preview in June 2026 in partnership with Red Hat, these images are now fully supported for production workflows in GitHub Actions. You can use RHEL images to run your workflows on the same operating system you deploy to, or as the foundation for custom images that include your required tools, dependencies, and configurations. To get started, create a new Linux x64 larger runner and choose your desired RHEL image under partner images. If you’ve been using RHEL images during the public preview, no action is required. Your existing runners and workflows will continue to work as-is. RHEL images are available for larger runners on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud plans. To learn more, see Managing larger runners and Using custom images . The post Red Hat Enterprise Linux runner images now generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
